content: Dr. Ayesha Motala, affiliated with the University of KwaZulu-Natal in Durban, South Africa, stated that as a public servant employed in a government institution, she seeks sponsorships from various organizations to attend scientific meetings, particularly when her abstracts are accepted for presentation. These sponsorships are solely for covering travel and accommodation expenses and do not entail any obligations to the sponsoring companies. For example, she received sponsorships amounting to a total of USD 26,000 for the following events: the International Diabetes Federation Congress in Abu Dhabi (December 2017) sponsored by Sanofi Aventis, the European Association for the Study of Diabetes Congress in Lisbon (September 2017) sponsored by Pfizer, and the American Diabetes Association meeting in San Diego (June 2018) sponsored by Boehringer Ingelheim. It was determined that these sponsorships posed minimal or insignificant conflicts of interest and were unlikely to affect her role as an external reviewer for the WHO guidelines. No further action was deemed necessary. Dr. Ronald C. Petersen from the Mayo Clinic in Rochester, USA, disclosed that he serves as a clinical trials consultant for five pharmaceutical companies. He receives less than USD 10,000 from four of these companies (Roche Inc., Merck Inc., Genentech Inc., and GE Healthcare) and less than USD 15,000 from Biogen Inc. as consultancy fees. It was concluded that these financial interests were unrelated to the topic of the guidelines and were unlikely to influence his contributions as an external reviewer. No further action was required. Professor Martin Prince from King’s College London, UK, declared that he receives research funding from the National Institute of Health Research (NIHR) in the UK, amounting to £7 million over four years. He serves as the principal investigator, with 20% of his salary costs covered by the grant. The research focuses on integrated primary healthcare for multimorbid conditions. This interest was deemed minimal and unlikely to affect his judgment in the development of the guidelines. No further action was necessary. Dr. Suzana Shahar from Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia, Selangor, Malaysia, disclosed a clinical trial agreement through her university with Biotropics, a company developing bio-resources into natural health products. The research evaluates the efficacy of Asian traditional herbs in improving cognition and mood, with funding of USD 100,000 between 2014 and 2018. This interest was considered minimal and unlikely to influence her role as an external reviewer. No further action was required. Dr. Huali Wang from the Dementia Care & Research Center at Peking University Institute of Mental Health, Beijing, China, declared that prior to 2016, she worked as a consultant with Neowave Inc. to develop a tablet-based cognitive training program. Additionally, she received USD 7,000 in travel support from Eisai China for attending Alzheimer’s Disease International (ADI) conferences before 2017. These interests were deemed minimal and unlikely to affect her contributions as an external reviewer. No further action was necessary. Dr. Emiliano Albanese from Università della Svizzera italiana, Switzerland, disclosed receiving research support from the Economic and Research Council UK as part of the STRIDE consortium, which focuses on dementia research in lowand middle-income countries. The funding, amounting to USD 50,000, is provided to his affiliated institution. This interest was considered minimal and unlikely to influence his role as an external reviewer. No further action was required. Ms. Hillary Doxford from the 3 Nations Dementia Working Group, UK, declared that she served on a grant review panel for the National Institute for Health Research (NIHR), assessing and prioritizing dementia research projects, for which she received £450. She is also a voluntary member of the Dementia Programme Board in the UK Department of Health and Social Care, representing individuals with lived experience. These interests were deemed minimal and unlikely to affect her contributions as an external reviewer. No further action was necessary. Dr. Elaine Rashbrook from Public Health England (PHE), UK, declared her employment as a Consultant Specialist in Life Course at PHE, a government agency supporting dementia risk reduction in alignment with government strategy. No financial value was identified for this work. It was determined that her role was provided in an individual capacity and did not represent any organization. This interest was deemed minimal and unlikely to influence her contributions as an external reviewer. No further action was required. Dr. Andrew Sommerlad from University College London, UK, disclosed receiving research funding from the Wellcome Trust in the form of a personal research fellowship to investigate whether social isolation is a risk factor for dementia. The funding amounted to £201,311 from 2016 to 2019. This interest was considered minimal and unlikely to affect his role as an external reviewer. No further action was necessary. External review group members with no relevant interests declared on their DOI forms or identified in their CVs include Abdullah Al Khatami (Saudi Arabia), Alistair Burns (UK), Linda Clare (UK), Jacqueline Dominguez (Philippines), Maelenn Guerchet (UK), Mariella Guerra (Peru), Luis Miguel F. Gutiérrez Robledo (Mexico), Vladimir Hachinski (Canada), Qurat ul Ain Khan (Pakistan), Sebastian Koehler (Netherlands), Jae-hong Lee (Korea), Gill Livingston (UK), Jean Claude Mbanya (Cameroon), James McKillop (UK), Rajat Ray (India), Helen Rochford Brennan (Ireland), Kate Swaffer (Australia), and Weili Xu (Finland). None of these individuals declared relevant interests or had any identified in their CVs. External partners with no relevant interests declared on their DOI forms or identified in their CVs include Mariagnese Barbera (Finland), Nicole A. Ee (Australia), Jenni Kumlala (Sweden), Ruth Peters (Australia), and Lidan Zheng (Australia). None of these individuals declared relevant interests or had any identified in their CVs.
